newsitem.title: USA: CBOT soybeans end lower on technical break in Nov.
newsitem.headline: CBOT soybeans end lower on technical break in Nov.

text.p: Technical selling which started when November faltered early just above $8.00 per bushel, drove CBOT soybean futures to a lower close, traders said.
"We couldn't maintain those levels and that was all it took to break it," said Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter Reynolds.
November soybeans early rallied to a session high of $8.02 per bushel but demand quickly waned which touched off a spate of broad-based selling, mainly fund sales.
"End of the month fund profit taking," said Steve Bruce of E.D. and F. Man International referring to the soy slide.

Soybeans rallied early on outlooks for dry weather over the near term in the Midwest. "We need rain, they (soy) definitely need rain," Lespinasse said. Meteorologists early Wednesday said the U.S. weather patterns remain volatile but agreed that no significant rain events were in sight for the Midwest over the near term.
"The bottom line is that the pattern is warmer than normal and drier than normal until further notice," said Jon Davis, Smith Barney meteorologist.
Soybeans closed four to 8-3/4 cents per bushel lower, with Sep down seven at $8.17. Nov was down seven at $7.88-3/4.
Traders said that current warm temperatures in the Midwest suggest the soybean crop is in no danger over the near term.
"Right now looking at the temperatures and the temperatures look good. Yes it's a little dry in a few spots but right now there are no problems," Bruce said.
USDA Monday said 80 percent of the U.S. soybean crop was in the critical pod setting stage of development as of Sunday, below the 84 percent pace a year ago and below the 85 percent average pace.
Merrill Lynch Futures sold four million bushels of November, Cargill Inc sold 2.5 million and ADM Investor Services sold two million November, they said.
Soybean futures volume was estimated at 59,000 contracts, up from 49,536 Tuesday, according to the CBOT.
In soybean options Smith Barney bought 2,000 January $8.50 calls at 26 to 29 cents and sold 500 January $8.00 to $8.75 call spreads at 21-1/2 cents.
"That is about the same as over three million January beans bought," a trader said.
Soybean options volume was estimated at 22,000, up from 17,139 Tuesday.
